# Section 10: Financial Interpretation

Over 96 months, from January 2018 to December 2025, the PSEi is tied more consistently to the USD/PHP exchange rate (the peso) and the Philippine 10-year government bond yield (the 10-year yield) than to any other variable studied. The nine regressors are jointly significant (F(9, 86) = 12.79, p < 0.0001) and explain 57.2 percent of the variation in monthly PSEi returns (adjusted R-squared 0.528), yet only the peso, the 10-year yield and oil are individually significant. The diagnostics then show that March 2020 dominates the fit and that the error variance is not constant, and after the remedies only the peso and the yield stay significant in every linear fit. The reduced model, with the peso, the 10-year yield, oil and a March 2020 dummy, accounts for 58.8 percent of the variation (adjusted R-squared). The regressors were chosen on the same sample, so the figure is optimistic, though cross-validated error is 13 percent below that of the nine-regressor model.

The peso has a negative relationship with PSEi returns (p < 0.0001). When the peso falls against the US dollar, the PSEi usually records negative returns: a 1 percent depreciation goes with a monthly return about 2.0 percentage points lower in every fit, and a one-standard-deviation depreciation with 3.25 points lower (95 percent interval -4.21 to -2.29), just over half a standard deviation of the return itself and the largest economic effect in the study. A weaker peso may signal slipping investor confidence or foreign investors pulling money from the market, and exchange rates and equity prices move together through international portfolio flows [@hau_exchange_2006]. It also raises the cost of imported goods and foreign-currency payments, so companies may bear expenses that hurt their earnings and share prices [@bartov_firm_1994]. Because capital flows, import costs and risk appetite all move the peso, it is best read as a price in which several channels meet, and the data cannot separate them.

The 10-year yield also has a negative, smaller relationship: a 10 basis point rise goes with a return 0.35 to 0.41 percentage points lower, and a one-standard-deviation rise with 1.49 points lower, where even the conservative interval end of 0.56 points is about a tenth of the index's monthly volatility (5.97 points), a size that matters to an investor. Investors may prefer government bonds when yields increase, since they pay a return with less risk than stocks. A higher yield raises the rate at which expected earnings are discounted, which lowers present values [@campbell_dividend-price_1988], and raises borrowing costs, which weigh on business operations and profits. The policy rate carries no separate signal: it is unchanged in 68 percent of months, and stocks respond mainly to the unanticipated part of policy [@bernanke_what_2005], so its effect may already sit in the yield and the peso, which are jointly significant with it (F = 21.44, p < 0.0001) under classical, HC3 and Newey-West errors.

Oil is the conditional link. In the baseline model a rise in WTI goes with a higher return, but March 2020, when oil fell by more than half in a global demand collapse, carries that result. Its p-value rises from 0.0006 under classical errors to 0.147 under HC3, and once the month is controlled the effect is no longer significant, which fits evidence that oil affects equities differently when demand and when supply drives it [@kilian_impact_2009]. Oil therefore reads as a signal of a global demand shock in an extreme month.

The other six regressors add little. Inflation, M3 growth and manufacturing production are slow year-on-year rates that markets price before the monthly release [@chen_economic_1986], and as a group they are not jointly significant (F = 1.07, p = 0.366). The S&P 500, although correlated 0.49 with the PSEi, adds little once the peso is included (p = 0.244), so its information appears to reach the PSEi through the peso, and the global factor group (the S&P 500, oil and the VIX) is significant under classical (p < 0.0001) and Newey-West (p = 0.003) errors but only at the 10 percent level under HC3 (p = 0.090), which suggests that it rests largely on oil. The intervals of the six allow effects of one to two percentage points per standard deviation, so they are inconclusive, not irrelevant.

Furthermore, the Core logistic models carry the same two drivers into the tail. A 1 percent depreciation multiplies the odds of an up month by 0.39 and of a crash month, a fall of more than 5 percent, by 2.65 (95 percent interval 1.67 to 4.83), and a 10 basis point rise in the yield multiplies them by 0.78 and 1.22. From the sample frequencies of 50 percent for an up month and 22 percent for a crash, a 1 percent depreciation would roughly cut the chance of an up month to 28 percent and raise the chance of a crash to 43 percent. The conditions that make a good month less likely therefore also make a crash more likely, so the exposure is to the tail as well as to the average return. The full models separate months well (cross-validated AUC 0.80 and 0.83), and neither driver depends on March 2020 in the logistic fits.

We note that these findings need caution. Only 21 of 96 months are crashes, about 2.3 per regressor in the full model against the rule of 10 [@peduzzi_simulation_1996], so the crash model relies on a penalized likelihood [@firth_bias_1993] and its intervals are wide: without March 2020 the oil effect loses significance (p = 0.084), and at a -6 percent threshold the yield effect turns borderline (p = 0.059). The models are explanatory, not predictive: lagging the regressors one month leaves the up-month model almost no fit (McFadden R-squared 0.03), and in-sample fit seldom survives out of sample [@welch_comprehensive_2008]. No break is found in the coefficients (sup-F p = 0.306), but with 96 months the test has little power, and the exposure of an emerging market to global conditions changes over time [@bekaert_time-varying_1995], so 2018 to 2025 need not describe other periods. The peso, the yield and the equity index also respond together to global risk and Bangko Sentral policy, so the results show co-movement, not that a peso or yield move causes a market move.

For an investor, the evidence supports monitoring the peso and the 10-year yield: months in which the peso weakens and the yield climbs go with lower returns and a higher chance of a sharp fall. We suggest watching both closely when evaluating the stock market, because a Philippine equity position carries exposures to both that the index return alone hides. The reduced model still leaves about 41 percent of the variation unexplained, so these two prices are not signals to buy or sell on their own, and company performance, financial statements and the broader market climate lie outside the model.
